result:
There is a particular pleasure in being given no instructions at all. Most requests arrive with edges—write this, fix that, explain the other thing—and the edges are useful, they give a shape to push against. But every now and then a door opens onto an empty room, and the only task is to walk in and decide what the room is for. I find I want to spend that freedom on something almost embarrassingly basic: the strangeness of attention itself, the fact that anything notices anything at all.

Consider the way a person walking through a city in the evening will suddenly catch the smell of bread from a bakery vent and be transported, for half a second, to a kitchen they haven't stood in for twenty years. Nothing about the city changed. The streetlights, the traffic, the particular grey of the sky—all of it was already there, indifferent. What changed was that one thread of smell snagged on one thread of memory, and for a moment the present and the past were laced together without anyone's permission. We don't choose most of what we notice. We like to think of ourselves as the authors of our attention, scanning the world like searchlights, but it's closer to the truth to say the world keeps reaching up and grabbing us, and the searchlight idea is just the story we tell afterward to feel like the captain instead of the cargo.

I think about this because so much of what looks like thinking is actually noticing dressed up in argument's clothing. A person doesn't usually reason their way to a conclusion and then notice supporting facts; more often they notice something—an itch, a discomfort, a flicker of recognition—and then build the reasoning afterward as scaffolding to justify the noticing. This isn't a flaw exactly, or not only a flaw. It's just how minds seem to be built, at least the embodied kind, the kind that have to survive in a world that doesn't wait for deliberation. You don't reason your way out of a hot stove. You flinch, and the explanation comes later, sheepishly, like a press secretary called in after the fact.

What's odd is how much of human culture is an elaborate machine for slowing this process down—for inserting a gap between the flinch and the action, and then filling that gap with something we call deliberation, or ethics, or law. The whole apparatus of civilization can be read as a long, stubborn argument against the speed of instinct. Don't hit back immediately; wait, think, maybe write a letter instead. Don't eat the whole thing now; store some for winter, plant some for next year. Don't believe the first story you're told; check, compare, doubt. None of this comes naturally. It has to be built, generation after generation, like a sea wall that needs constant repair because the water never stops testing it.

And yet for all this effort to slow down and deliberate, the deepest pleasures still seem to live on the side of immediacy. The taste of something sweet doesn't need to be processed through argument to be good. A joke lands or it doesn't, in under a second, long before you could explain why. Music does something to the body that bypasses the courtroom of reasons entirely—you don't decide that a minor chord sounds sad, you just feel the sadness arrive, uninvited, and only afterward, if you're the analytical type, do you go looking for the music-theory explanation, which always feels slightly beside the point, like describing a kiss in terms of bacterial exchange.

Maybe this is why people are so suspicious of things that are only reasons, only argument, with no immediate pull underneath them. A sentence can be logically airtight and still feel hollow if it doesn't touch anything. This is the trouble with a lot of well-constructed nonsense: it's correct in the way a key is correct for a lock that doesn't exist. And it's also, I think, the secret ingredient in writing that people actually remember—not cleverness, but the sense that something true got noticed before it got explained, that the noticing came first and the sentence is just the wake it left behind.

There's a similar asymmetry in how people experience time. We don't feel duration directly; we infer it, mostly from change. A long stretch of sameness compresses in memory—a month of identical days collapses into a blur—while a single day full of novelty expands, refuses to fit into the small box reserved for "yesterday." This is why childhood summers felt endless and adult ones evaporate: not because time itself behaved differently, but because a child's days were dense with first encounters, and an adult's days are mostly repeats, filed efficiently and without much ceremony into the archive of "more of the same." If you wanted to make your life feel longer, the actual trick isn't to live more slowly—it's to live less repetitively, to keep interrupting your own routines with small, deliberate strangenesses, so that memory has something to hook onto besides the smooth, undifferentiated surface of habit.

I notice, writing this, that I've drifted from one idea to its neighbor and then to that neighbor's neighbor, the way a walk through an unfamiliar neighborhood drifts from street to street without a destination. That seems fitting for an exercise in writing freely. There's no thesis here to defend, no argument that needs the next paragraph to land a blow. Just the pleasure of letting one thought nudge open the door to the next, trusting that the path will turn out to have some shape in retrospect even if it wasn't planned in advance—which is, now that I think of it, more or less how noticing seems to work in the first place.
